# ob-13 — Floating-point columns do not round-trip exactly

Floating-point columns restore to the same numeric value: new manifests transform them with exact decimal arithmetic on BigInteger instead of double.

**Findings:** Obfuscator/ObfuscationEngine.cs ObfuscateFloating/DeobfuscateFloating: (x*Scale+Shift) then (y-Shift)/Scale changes the last digits of G17 output (e.g. 131.60538314346292 -> 131.60538314346289) in scripts/test-local.sh sample output; README does not document floats as approximate and test-local.sh does not compare restored CSVs · **Size:** S · **Tree:** core,tests

**2026-10-08** — Ready for review: branch ob-13-exact-floats (f40d59c claim, a9b3b5d implementation). Behaviour change: new manifests (version 2.2) transform floating columns with exact decimal arithmetic (new internal ExactDecimal, BigInteger mantissa x 10^exponent); specs record FloatScheme exact-decimal/v1, ExactScale (4 decimals) and ExactShift (4 significant digits), omitted when null so pre-2.2 checksums verify; pre-2.2 manifests keep the double path. Restores the same numeric value, not always the same text (5.0 -> 5, 1,000.5 -> 1000.5). Cells beyond 1000 significant digits or |exponent| ~1100 take the string path and count as unparsed (--strict rejects). Edited float cells fail without echoing the value. README documents exactness, normalization, and that exact output reveals roughly how many decimal places the original had. Checks: regression FloatingColumn_RoundTripsToSameNumericValue failed on main (131.60538314346292 -> 131.6053831434628) and passes; round-trip theory over 215 values x 6 transforms (incl. 5e-324, 1e300, -MaxValue, infinite shift), ExactDecimal parse/format/reject, tamper, unknown scheme, legacy spec, unbounded-cell tests pass; dotnet test Obfuscator.slnx 177/177; scripts/test-local.sh exit 0 with new assert_restored (cells byte-equal or numerically equal; plain cmp failed only on -40.0/5.0 normalization); slicer check passed. macOS only locally. No follow-ups filed.

trust: unverified; by: Jon R

**Not in this slice:** byte-identical text restoration (formatting such as `1.50` or `1,000.5` may be normalized); integer, date, or string transforms; changing how pre-2.2 manifests restore floats.

## Why

`ObfuscateFloating`/`DeobfuscateFloating` compute `y = x*Scale + Shift` in `double` and write G17, so `(y-Shift)/Scale` is not the original: `131.60538314346292` comes back as `131.60538314346289`, and small values next to a large shift lose low bits. The README calls obfuscation reversible and `scripts/test-local.sh` never compares restored CSVs, so nothing catches it.

## Files

Obfuscator/ExactDecimal.cs (new); Obfuscator/ObfuscationEngine.cs; Obfuscator/Models.cs; Obfuscator.Tests/ObfuscatorTests.cs; README.md; scripts/test-local.sh.

## Failing tests

Obfuscating and deobfuscating a float column containing `131.60538314346292` with a deterministic key returns the same number (fails on main). Random doubles, `0`, `-0`, `5e-324`, `1e-30`, `1e300`, `double.MaxValue`, thousands separators and exponent forms round-trip to the same numeric value across scales and shifts. An edited obfuscated float cell fails without echoing the value. A spec without `FloatScheme` still uses the legacy double path.

## Implement

Add an internal `ExactDecimal` (BigInteger mantissa x 10^exponent) with exact parse of the `NumberStyles.Float | AllowThousands` grammar (no NaN/Infinity, bounded exponent), add/subtract/multiply, exact division, and normalized invariant formatting. Float specs gain `FloatScheme = "exact-decimal/v1"`, `ExactScale` (4 decimals) and `ExactShift` (4 significant digits), null-omitted so old checksums verify; manifest version 2.2. Cells that do not parse exactly take the string path and count as unparsed. Document numeric-value (not text) restoration and the digit-count leak in the README.

## Check

`dotnet test Obfuscator.slnx`; `scripts/test-local.sh` exits 0 and its new restored-vs-source comparison passes for both sample CSVs; `slicer check`.

Pre-2.2 manifests (no `FloatScheme`) must still deobfuscate with the existing double transform.
